overview: “Hindu kingdoms” is a broad imported map label, not the name of one ancient empire. Its outlines jump between northern, central and southern regions from 500 BCE to 800 CE. They neither locate every kingdom accurately nor identify everyone’s religion. Buddhist, Jain and diverse Brahmanical traditions shared these landscapes. The examples below concern particular places and periods; the atlas also has separate Maurya, Gupta, Pallava and Chalukya cards.

periods.title: Early states and expanding networks
periods.summary: Regional states and cities developed alongside larger empires. Southern communities followed their own political trajectories.

periods.title: Trade and regional courts
periods.summary: Southern maritime networks and Tamil literature flourished, while Gupta rulers consolidated a large northern kingdom in the fourth century.

periods.title: Several influential centres
periods.summary: Harsha governed a large northern kingdom, while other regional courts and Buddhist institutions also flourished.

periods.title: New powers and lasting institutions
periods.summary: Rashtrakuta ascendancy in the Deccan formed part of continuing regional change. The imported cutoff is not a common political ending.

items.text: Around the beginning of this map span, northern India contained powerful regional states often called mahajanapadas. Magadha became the core of the later Mauryan empire. Buddhism and Jainism developed alongside Brahmanical traditions. A label based on one modern religious category cannot adequately describe this political and intellectual variety.

The Guptas consolidated much of northern India in the fourth century CE. Their era saw Sanskrit literature and religious sculpture flourish, including Buddhist images. In the south, maritime commerce connected communities with Rome and Southeast Asia. These overlapping histories belonged to different courts, ports and communities, rather than a single government directing the whole subcontinent.

Harsha, who ruled in the seventh century, became a major northern king and a patron of Buddhist learning. His court belonged to a world of Sanskrit literature, diplomatic travel and competing regional powers. The Chalukyas were important rivals to the south; the map’s enormous shared outline should not be read as Harsha’s personal territory.

Southern courts also supported distinctive literary cultures. Tamil devotional poets addressed Shiva and Vishnu in a regional language, while Pallava, Pandya and Chalukya rulers sponsored monuments and religious institutions. Their communities included Buddhists and Jains as well. Shared artistic ideas could travel between rival kingdoms without making their governments, languages or beliefs identical.

sections.title: An excavated town beside the Vaigai

items.text: Keeladi, near Madurai in southern India, preserves an early historic town associated with the Sangam age. Excavators found ovens, pots, brick remains and grooved roof tiles. These objects bring the story down from royal courts to cooking, shelter and maintenance. The site’s evidence spans layers; every object should not be assigned the same year.

A terracotta well uncovered at Keeladi in 2021 had interlocking rings and raised rope-like decoration. One exposed ring measured 77 centimetres across. Its decorated upper part may once have been visible above ground. A working water installation could receive ornamental attention too, rather like making the useful corner of a home look nice.

Spindle whorls, beads, bangles, dice and gaming pieces were among the Keeladi finds. They point to textile work, adornment and recreation within the same settlement. A spindle whorl helped turn fibre into thread; the small game pieces remind us that ancient life contained play as well as chores. The finds do not identify each player’s age.

sections.title: A king’s words and places of learning

items.text: A copperplate grant from Banskhera bears a striking royal formula. In scholarly Roman transliteration, its Sanskrit begins “svahasto mama”, meaning “my own hand”, followed by Harsha’s royal titles and name. The inscription dates to his year 22, approximately 628 CE. This is one northern royal document, not a sample of every language spoken across the map.

The Banskhera plate also names an engraver, Isvara, and two beneficiaries of the grant. The royal formula appears in enlarged, ornamental letters. Thus the surviving record brings together a king’s authority, a craftsperson’s work and named recipients. The words claiming the king’s own hand should not be confused with a claim that he personally cut every letter into copper.

Nalanda in Bihar became a major Buddhist residential and teaching institution from the fifth century CE onward. Its monasteries combined places to live with places to study and worship. This is an important reminder that the areas gathered under the map’s “Hindu kingdoms” label also contained influential Buddhist communities and centres of learning.

Nalanda’s visible ruins contain many generations of construction, including eleven monasteries and fourteen temples within the protected property. Archaeologists excavated and conserved the site in the early twentieth century. Some modern repair bricks carry discreet dates. Looking closely means separating ancient building, later additions and the work that keeps fragile ruins standing today.

The late-seventh-century Chinese monk Yijing described chewing a small piece of wood to clean the teeth. He reported that even children around three years old were taught the habit. His account mixes observations with advice for Buddhist readers; it preserves a memorable family routine without proving that every household followed it in exactly the same way.

Yijing also described checking water for tiny creatures and straining it through cloth. Monks were supposed to return trapped insects safely to water. The stated aim was to avoid harming living beings. A filter here belonged to religious discipline, so it should not be mistaken for evidence that people understood modern germ theory.

In Yijing’s account, images of Hariti, a protective mother figure, received offerings of food in monasteries. She was shown with a baby and other children, and people who wanted children approached her. Such practices connected religious institutions with family hopes. The story’s promises of answered prayers are beliefs recorded by the traveller, not medical evidence.

Medical knowledge travelled beyond these kingdoms. The Bower manuscript, written on birch bark and dated broadly to the fourth through sixth centuries, preserves Sanskrit medical material related to Indian traditions. It was found near Kucha in Central Asia, outside this map’s footprint. Its survival shows the movement of texts and healing knowledge, rather than the services available in every Indian village.

At Pattadakal, Queen Lokamahadevi commissioned the Virupaksha temple around 740 to commemorate her husband’s southern victories. The monuments bring together architectural forms associated with northern and southern India. A queen’s patronage and the work of designers, stonecutters and sculptors became visible in a building that survived the court that commissioned it.

At Ellora, the Kailasa temple was cut from living rock rather than assembled entirely from separate blocks. Its carvings include Ravana trying to lift Shiva’s mountain. Rashtrakuta patronage supported this eighth-century achievement. The wider cave group also contains Buddhist monuments and later Jain caves, so everything visible at Ellora does not belong to one dynasty or to years before 800.

ending.text: The imported label stops at 800 CE, but there was no common fall of “the Hindu kingdoms”. Rashtrakuta, Pala and Gurjara-Pratihara power continued into later centuries, and religious communities, languages and institutions kept changing. Individual dynasties had their own endings; this umbrella record should not replace those histories or imply that a population disappeared.
